w: 1 Regeneration = new bone, new cementum and new PDL, all three; a long junctional epithelium is repair A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this Regeneration = new bone + new cementum + new PDL over a pathologically exposed root. Bone fill alone isn't regeneration; a long junctional epithelium against the root is repair. Periodontal regeneration is the formation of new bone, new cementum and new periodontal ligament, together a new functional attachment apparatus, over a pathologically exposed root surface (the 1996 World Workshop's definition, on the slides). In class: "three different tissues that have to all regenerate in harmony with each other. It can't just be bone alone." If only bone came back, something else would sit between the bone and the root: epithelium, or ligament that isn't attached. The slide sets regeneration against repair, healing that does not restore the original architecture and function. After a flap or root planing, a root usually heals by repair: a long junctional epithelium lies against the root instead of new cementum with inserting ligament fibers, and a pocket lined by epithelium is a pocket again. 2 3-wall (most contained) defects regenerate best: more walls, a steeper angle, more depth Hint + review guide · 9 questions in the bank Know this 3-wall defects are the most amenable to regeneration: the walls contain the graft and the clot and give more bony surface to heal from. More walls, more contained, more predictable. Walls, angle and depth: more walls, a steeper (narrower) angle and a deeper defect regenerate better (the slide: deeper than 3 mm, 25 degrees or less). A narrow defect fills better but is harder to instrument, so there's an optimum. Regenerate vertical (infrabony) defects. Horizontal bone loss has no defect and no walls, so it isn't a regeneration case. The walls matter because the more walls there are, the more contained the defect: what you put in it stays there, and there is more bony surface to influence the wound. "Potentially the most amenable to regeneration are the three wall defects, the most contained ones." The angle of the walls matters too: a steeper, narrower defect fills more completely, but it is harder to instrument, so there is an optimum between the two. And so does the depth: a shallow defect may regenerate, but other therapies may be more predictable for it. His summary: "more walls, better. An angle that is more steep is better. And the depth of the defect is also important." Flat or horizontal bone loss isn't amenable to regeneration: "There's just no defect to fill." The slide behind that summary gives the numbers: defects with a depth greater than 3 mm and a radiographic defect angle of 25 degrees or less were reported to be most amenable to conventional GTR-based regeneration; non-supportive anatomy, a predominantly 1-wall defect, is a risk factor for failure; and a 1-wall rather than a 2-wall defect and a thin, scalloped gingival biotype were the risk factors for more recession at the midfacial after minimally invasive regenerative surgery. He said the slide's list of studies is there as his sources, "not there for you to read all these studies": know what they support. A 2021 systematic review on the next slide (Nibali) agrees: deeper defects with narrower angles and more walls gained more CAL and radiographic bone 12 months after regenerative surgery. 3 No root canal needed to regenerate, only clean roots (a root canal when vitality is compromised) A professor's hint · 3 questions in the bank Know this No root canal is needed to regenerate a defect: clean roots are. A root canal is done only when the tooth's vitality is compromised, as it can be when a defect reaches toward the apex. A mandibular canine next to the lateral incisor had a vertical defect. It had a root canal with two canals, which is uncommon in a mandibular canine, and two canals mean two roots formed and fused together, usually into an H-shaped root with a concavity. At surgery, through a small "peekaboo" flap, the defect was what the radiograph suggested, a 3-wall component and a 2-wall component, and in the concavity was a streak of calculus: a hard place for the patient to clean, and the reason the defect was there. The root canal wasn't why the tooth could be regenerated. You don't need a root canal to do regeneration: "generally for a tooth to do regeneration, all you need is clean roots." A root canal is done when the tooth's vitality is compromised, as it may be when a defect reaches toward the apex. 4 The AAP decision tree (he said to study it) A professor's hint · 7 questions in the bank Know this Study the AAP decision tree (Reynolds 2015): fix the patient first; under 3 mm, no regeneration; a narrow 3-wall or circumferential defect takes a graft, a membrane or a biologic; a wide or 2-wall defect a reinforced membrane or a graft with a membrane or biologic; a 1-wall defect combination therapy; high esthetic risk, no membrane. The decision tree from the AAP Regeneration Workshop (Reynolds, 2015) is in the handout, and he told the class to study it. What it says: understand your defect, how deep the pocket is, what the bony morphology is and how many walls it has, and then choose the therapy. It starts with the patient: address first uncontrolled systemic conditions, tobacco use and other behavioral issues, and inadequate oral hygiene (the same factors that ruled furcation regeneration out in Session 5). After initial therapy and any occlusal trauma or mobility management, assess the site: probing depth and CAL, bleeding on probing, mobility and fremitus, the osseous architecture clinically and on radiographs, and any restorative, endodontic or orthodontic work. An intrabony defect under 3 mm isn't a regeneration case: with probing depths of 5 mm or less and no bleeding, consider non-surgical management; with probing depths over 5 mm, consider osseous surgery. For a defect of 3 mm or more, predictability runs 3-wall, then circumferential or 2-wall, then 1-wall, and narrow beats wide. If the prognosis with treatment is unfavorable, or poor to hopeless, the answer is extraction and tooth replacement. Otherwise regeneration follows the defect: a 3-wall or circumferential defect under 2 mm wide takes a bone graft, a GTR membrane or a biologic; one 3 mm or wider, or a 2-wall defect, takes a reinforced GTR membrane, a bone graft plus a GTR membrane, or a bone graft plus a biologic; a 1-wall defect takes combination therapy or a cellular bone allograft. Esthetic risk is weighed alongside. With low risk (a low smile line, a thick biotype, a full papilla, under 5 mm from the contact to the interproximal bone crest), proceed. With high risk (a high smile line, a thin biotype, papilla loss or more than 6 mm from the contact to the crest), proceed only if the patient accepts the esthetic risk, avoid a GTR membrane, and consider soft-tissue augmentation. 5 Clean the root first: calculus, scaling and root planing, removing granulomatous tissue A professor's hint · 3 questions in the bank Know this Wherever there's calculus there are bacteria (the red and orange complexes can sit straight on it), so the root must be clean before anything goes in: root planing first, closed, then the roots are inspected and finished at surgery. Whether it worked is judged by the tissue's response. Granulomatous tissue (the diseased tissue; granulation tissue is the healing one) won't turn into bone and blocks bone healing. Removing it exposes the bony walls, which then help the defect heal. His opening case was a molar with a deep vertical (infrabony) defect, the two words for the same thing: they describe the shape of bone loss that wraps down beside the root, and with it comes a deep pocket. The first problem in that defect is bacteria. The root wasn't smooth: there was calculus on it, and wherever there is calculus there are bacteria. Calculus is porous and hard to clean, and it lets the pathogenic red and orange complex bacteria sit straight on the root, without the early colonizers a biofilm normally needs first. So the contamination has to go, and the way to clean a root is scaling and root planing ("If you want to answer a question right in perio, the answer is scaling and root planing"). Usually it is done closed first; at the regenerative procedure the flap gives direct access to see the roots and finish cleaning them. "The most important thing to understand is that it has to be clean." The soft tissue in the defect isn't PDL (that's gone) and isn't bone. It is granulomatous tissue, the diseased tissue (granulation tissue is the healing tissue, a different thing). It has to be removed: left in place it won't turn into bone or support and it gets in the way of bone healing into the site. Removing it exposes the bony walls of the defect, and those walls can then contribute to healing a site that is new and has to fill with tissue. 6 Vertical defects regenerate, horizontal bone loss doesn't; a defect obvious on a film has usually lost a wall A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank Know this Bone loss obvious on a film means more than 50% of the mineral is gone, usually including the buccal or lingual wall. The best candidates probe deep (an 8 mm pocket) with only a faint shadow. The decision comes from probing and radiographs; the walls are confirmed at surgery. You don't raise a flap to decide whether a defect can be regenerated: you decide from clinical measurements and radiographs. The chart gives the probing depths and, if the gingival margin is recorded, the attachment levels, so you know where the deep pockets are. Radiographs show defects differently than you might think. For bone loss to be obvious to the eye on a film, more than 50% of the mineral content has to be lost, and for most periodontal defects that means the buccal or lingual wall is gone: "by the time we see it on the radiograph, it likely is not a three-wall defect." The defects that are really good for regeneration are the ones that probe deep (an 8 mm pocket, say) where the radiograph shows only a faint shadow. A radiograph is a flat picture of a three-dimensional defect, as the deck's dry-skull films of 3-, 2- and 1-wall defects on the same molar show (Zengin, 2015), so the walls are confirmed at surgery, once the flap is raised and the defect is debrided. 7 The race for the space: epithelium wins unless a GTR membrane keeps it out A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this Without a barrier the flap's epithelium wins and the site heals as a pocket again (a long junctional epithelium). Bone is slow but predictable when it's still. GTR's membrane keeps the flap's epithelium and connective tissue out so bone and ligament can fill the defect. If you simply raise a flap, clean the defect and suture the flap back, "whatever tissue is the fastest in migrating into that defect will win the race to the space." That is the flap's epithelium: it migrates straight down the root toward the bone faster than anything else, and the flap's connective tissue is faster than bone too. Bone heals slowly but very predictably, as long as it isn't moving: a broken leg in a cast heals in about six weeks, where a cut in the skin is gone in a week, and an implant held still by its threads integrates. If epithelium reaches the base of the defect, the result is a pocket again, where bacteria thrive out of reach of the patient's and your cleaning. So regeneration means excluding epithelium and helping the slow tissues win. GTR sets up the race for the space. The potential to heal is in the defect: bone, and a little ligament space at the base, but those are the slow tissues; the fast ones are in the flap. So a barrier membrane goes between the defect and the flap, keeping out the flap's epithelium and connective tissue and letting the tissues we want repopulate the wound and decide what it becomes. The classic studies of the early 1980s wrapped laboratory filters around teeth and showed that bone could grow back; when he went to dental school, he was taught it couldn't. Early membranes had to be taken back out; today's collagen barriers are bioabsorbed: they stay a while, influence the healing and go away. 8 Only histology proves regeneration; probing and radiographs are surrogates A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank Regeneration is evaluated three ways: histology, clinical measurements and radiographs. "The real evaluation of regeneration should be histological," but very few patients allow it, so clinical measurements and radiographs serve as surrogates. Only histology, a section of the tooth with its surrounding tissue, can show new cementum with inserting PDL fibers and new bone, and so prove true regeneration; a probe can't tell new attachment from a long junctional epithelium, and a radiograph shows bone fill, not attachment. Digital subtraction radiography takes two standardized radiographs from different times, inverts one and overlays it on the other, so everything that stayed the same cancels out and only what changed shows. It is the work that brought him to Birmingham. Dr. Geurs and colleagues used it to evaluate a bioresorbable membrane (Chaves, Geurs, Reddy and Jeffcoat, 1996): the subtraction image lit up the bone gained between the presurgical film and the one at 6 months. In that study, a patient with a hopeless tooth agreed to have its defect regenerated, then the tooth removed for an implant: a notch cut in the root at the calculus, where there had been no bone, showed new PDL, new bone and a little new cementum. Histological evidence of regeneration in a human. At high magnification the new ligament isn't quite the ligament around a healthy tooth, but it is functional and resists breakdown over time. 9 Open flap debridement is the baseline (about a millimeter) every therapy must beat A professor's hint · 3 questions in the bank Know this Open flap debridement is the baseline: a little fill at the base and about a millimeter of attachment (the slide: PD about 7 to 4 mm, CAL gain about 1.5 mm, bone about 1 mm). Every regenerative therapy is judged by how much it adds. The baseline is open flap debridement. Open the defect, clean it and close it, and it heals one way or another: a little bone fill at the base (most likely in the 3-wall part at the bottom) and a little attachment gain, so "we're almost guaranteed by just cleaning it out to get a millimeter." Whatever is added has to outperform that. Across four studies on the slide (Froum 1981, Renvert 1985, Yukna 1985 and Laurell's 1998 meta-analysis), defects 3.4 to 4.3 mm deep started at probing depths of about 6.3 to 7.4 mm and ended at about 3.5 to 4.1 mm, with 1.3 to 1.5 mm of CAL gain and 0.7 to 1.2 mm of bone gain; Laurell's 305 defects went from 7.0 to 4.0 mm with 1.5 mm of CAL gain and 1.1 mm of bone gain. The probing depth fell 3 mm but the attachment level only 1.5 mm, because the rest of the pocket reduction is recession. It is historical data: other therapies now do much better. 10 Grafts and biologics: DFDBA exposes BMP, EMD (porcine amelogenins, consent), rhPDGF-BB with β-TCP Hint + review guide · 13 questions in the bank Know this EMD (mostly amelogenins, the proteins of Hertwig's root sheath) is harvested from developing teeth of miniature swine, so it's disclosed and consented. Any donor product is disclosed too, as a processed donor product, and the patient may say no. Enamel matrix derivative (EMD) goes back to embryology and Hertwig's epithelial root sheath. Its proteins, mostly amelogenins, the proteins of enamel formation and periodontal attachment formation during tooth development, are harvested from the developing teeth of miniature swine, a species genetically close to us (in humans they could only come from a developing wisdom tooth), then processed. Applied to a defect they set off a healing cascade like development, and he has seen "amazing healing" from EMD alone, without a bone graft. Alone or with a graft, EMD gives outcomes similar to GTR. Because it is porcine-derived, the patient has to be told and has to consent (it has been discussed with leaders of religions that avoid pork, but it is each patient's decision). The same goes for any donor product: say what you are using and why, call it a processed donor product, note that disease transmission isn't documented with these grafts, and let the patient say yes or no. A colleague who placed donor dermis in a priest without telling him had to take it out again. From the exam-review guide: rhPDGF-BB, recombinant human platelet-derived growth factor BB, is chemotactic and mitogenic for bone and PDL cells and angiogenic, so it drives revascularization; it is paired with a beta-TCP scaffold, an osteoconductive matrix that keeps soft tissue from collapsing into the defect and stabilizes the clot. Grafts are named by where they come from: an autograft from the patient, an allograft from another human (DFDBA), a xenograft from another species, such as bovine bone, and an alloplast, a synthetic material such as beta-tricalcium phosphate. 11 What to expect: the defect fills, vertical to horizontal, and the tooth is kept A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank Know this What to expect: the defect fills in ("my expectation is that I can fill in this defect"), not bone back to 1.5 mm from the CEJ. A vertical defect becomes a maintainable horizontal one, and the prognosis changes. A dense crest on later films means stability; a fuzzy crest means activity. The result (1993) was a shallow, maintainable pocket, and on the radiograph the defect filled in: a vertical defect became a horizontal one. That is the expectation, to fill the defect, not to grow bone back to within 1.5 mm of the CEJ where it belongs. It changed the tooth's prognosis, and a canine is worth it: the canine is "the cornerstone of the dentition," giving canine guidance so the laterals and posterior teeth aren't stressed ("canines are gold"). Because of the concavity, this patient should use an interdental brush, whose bristles spread into it, rather than floss, which bridges over the concavity and misses its depth. His patient Jeffrey had a deep defect (a 10 mm pocket) and an exostosis on the facial of the same quadrant. Dr. Geurs took off the exostosis, harvested the patient's own bone from it, packed it into the defect and covered it with a membrane: combination therapy, a scaffold (and possibly some cells) in the defect with a membrane over it. A bone graft under a membrane also holds the space, so the membrane can't collapse into the defect. The papilla didn't fully come back: raising tissue off a tooth and putting it back heals with a little recession, especially interproximally, a compromise of this therapy. The defect filled and leveled out, and it was still there on radiographs at 1, 20 and 25 years. On the later films the crest looks dense, sometimes called a crestal lamina dura, which goes with less activity and stability; a fuzzy crest, as before treatment, means activity and resorption. (Seeing Jeffrey every three months for years, his team was also the first to notice his cognitive decline: dentists see patients more often than physicians do.) 12 A still tooth and good technique: splint mobility, minimally invasive access A professor's hint · 3 questions in the bank Know this A mobile tooth is stabilized before regeneration: he splinted his 2022 EMD case with composite on the lingual. A defect heals when the tooth is still, like a broken bone. One of his EMD cases, from 2022, had almost no bone left and was very mobile. "Mobility is not a good thing during healing": a tooth that moves won't heal, like a leg out of its cast. So he splinted it with composite on the lingual, then placed EMD in the defect. The patient never came back for maintenance until a wisdom tooth abscess in 2025, and the bone was still there; the tooth, which had been slightly super-erupted, needed only a little occlusal adjustment. Splinting and regeneration together saved a tooth that might not have survived a treatment-planning session. 13 Furcations are harder: the root surface contributes no cells A professor's hint · 1 question in the bank Know this Furcations regenerate less predictably than intrabony defects with walls: most of the defect is root, which contributes no cells. Furcations are a different story. A furcation defect has a bony base, and the rest of it is root surface. A clean root lets tissue migrate over it, but it never contributes cells: it is "kind of a dead surface in healing," which makes furcations harder to treat. 14 Risk factors: 1-wall anatomy, a thin scalloped biotype, smoking, plaque, the root Core of the slides · 8 questions in the bank The periodontal regeneration risk assessment for intrabony defects (Levine, 2023), which he called a good summary of where your risk is, rates four groups of factors as low, medium or high risk. Patient factors: medical status (healthy, uneventful healing is low; compromised healing is high); smoking (a nonsmoker is low, a light smoker of 10 cigarettes a day or fewer is medium, more than 10 a day is high); plaque control by full-mouth plaque score (15% or less is low, 16 to 24% medium, 25% or more high); compliance with supportive periodontal care (compliant, erratic or poor); and realistic or unrealistic expectations. Tooth factors: the site's periodontal risk score; whether occlusal trauma and mobility are controllable; the endodontic condition (a vital tooth whose defect doesn't reach the apex, or adequate root canal treatment, is low; existing root canal therapy needs careful evaluation and is medium; a defect reaching the apex of a vital tooth, inadequate root canal treatment or a nonvital tooth is high); the root surface (flat is low, concave medium, two fused roots high); intact soft tissue or soft-tissue defects; and the gingival phenotype (thick is low; thin with a band of keratinized tissue 2 mm or wider is medium; thin with a narrow band or none is high). Defect factors: a 3-wall, narrow, deep defect is low, a 2-wall defect medium, and a 1-wall, wide, shallow defect high; no furcation involvement is low, Class I or II medium, Class III high; the defect must be cleansable through surgical access (anterior is low, posterior medium); and a contained defect, with 1 or 2 sides of the root involved, is low, while a non-contained defect, with 3 or more sides involved, is high. Operator factors: experience, environmental stress, and whether a checklist is used. Also flagged in class His two objectives: which defects can be regenerated (vertical, contained defects with walls) and what to expect (fill of the defect, a shallower, maintainable pocket, a better prognosis). Doing the surgery takes a specialist's training; recognizing the defect and referring is the general dentist's part. Surgical technique matters most: get access, clean the defect, place the material and close without disrupting the blood supply ("open the door, put stuff in, close the door"). With the right technique, DFDBA, the patient's own bone or both can all regenerate. DFDBA, a demineralized donor bone allograft, exposes its bone morphogenetic protein: a scaffold and a growth factor at once. Without its calcium it doesn't show on a film until bone forms around it (little at two and a half months). Asked if the patient's own bone is better: the evidence doesn't show it. A processed donor graft exposes its BMP better and goes in clean, so it's a toss-up. Autogenous bone is used particulated (scraped or milled), not processed; he likes it because it's already there. Regenerating a defect can keep a tooth for decades; an implant is for a tooth that can't be kept. General dentists have to recognize these defects and refer, or the periodontist never sees them. You can skip Said of the defect-morphology slide: the studies listed on it (Klein, Tonetti, Cortellini, Garrett, Cosyn, the AAP review) and their numbers aren't for memorizing. Know what they support: depth, the number of walls and the angle of the walls decide how well a defect regenerates.
